3	# What the revival changed in Fortress, and whose Fortress the skill describes
4	
5	## How to read this
6	
7	- Short lists. Numbers as K or M. A term is defined where it first appears.
8	- **The team**: the Sun Labs designers. **The team's tree**: this repository at `a874948ac`, their last commit (2012-08-31). **The revival**: every commit after it.
9	- **Walk**: the interpreter, `bin/fortress P.fss`. **The compiled path**: `fortress compile` then `fortress run`; it makes JVM bytecode. **The checker**: the static type checker, written in Scala; it runs on the compiled path only.
10	- **The library**: the Fortress files in `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`. There are two. The interpreter's, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, is called **the one library** here, because the curator chose it to become the only one. The compiler's own, **the prelude** (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), is deleted at the **switch-over**, the day the checker accepts the one library (POSITIONS, "The library route."; "The compiler prelude's leftovers go at the switch-over.").
11	- **Batch and rung**: a batch is one run of the climb workflow; a rung is one worker's piece of it. Batches are named 1 to 10 and 3.5, 6b, 7R, 7C, 6.5, 6.5b, N and 7b, after "the ladder climb" (eight rungs, 09-17) and "the repair batch" (09-18). Each batch's record is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/RECORD.md`; batches 1 and 2 have `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-1.md` and `-2.md`. Which commits each batch landed is in `record-growth/landings.csv` (beside this note) and in section A10.
12	- **Row**: a line of the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, cited by its number.
13	- **POSITIONS** holds the curator's decisions, **FACTS** what is established, both in `explorations/coordinator/`. A cited title is the entry's bold opening. **Answer N** is one of the curator's numbered answers of 2026-09-26 to 09-29 (answers 7 to 10 here).
14	- **Callout, S1 form, Appendix I**: how the revival changes the specification. A printed callout sits at the changed passage, and an entry in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`) quotes the original and gives the reason (POSITIONS, "The S1 form"). `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised specification: the Working Draft of 2011-02-02, byte for byte as the team left it.
15	- **Marks**. **[V]**: a programmer writing Fortress would notice it: a different answer, a program refused or accepted, or a different library declaration. **[I]**: internal.
16	- The tag `sealed-tree` is `75cca6683` (2026-09-16), the last commit before the revival edited the original sources. Its message: each later edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus (POSITIONS, "Test first, the test kept.").
17	- Evidence from the team's tree is cited as `a874948ac:path:line`, read with `git show a874948ac:path`.
18	
19	## A. What the revival changed
20	
21	### A0. The size of it
22	
23	- 122 commits touched `ProjectFortress/`, `Library/`, `Specification/` or `build.xml` after `a874948ac`. 28 came before the tag (2026-08-18 to 08-23), 94 after it (2026-09-17 to 10-03). None has touched those paths since 10-03 (checked at `bb54e2113`).
24	- Lines changed after the tag, generated files left out: walk +2.8K and -0.1K; the checker +1.2K and -0.2K; code generator, run time and natives +1.0K and -0.2K; the one library and the builtin files +3.0K and -2.1K (the ranges were respelled); the specification's text +4.7K and -0.6K; new tests +12K lines.
25	- The parser grammars (`*.rats`) are unchanged. The syntax tree description `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` gained 5 lines, one node.
26	- 43 of the team's own test and demo files have changed lines: 30 in `tests/`, 4 in `library_tests/`, 9 in `demos/`. New files: 146 in `tests/`, 491 in `compiler_tests/`, 32 in `library_tests/`. The suites: about 1.4K tests in `testFast` and 382 in `testSystem` on the team's tree, first run with the build moved to JDK 8 (`explorations/test-baseline-jdk8.md`); 1.8K and 516 at batch 10's gate (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-10/gate/summary.txt`).
27	- Per batch, what each changed in Fortress against what it recorded beside it, up to batch 6.5b: `postmortem-2026-09-29/characterization.md`. The landing paragraphs: `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`, first section (batches 8 to 10), and `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover-history.md` (the repair batch to 7b). The plan's phases: `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, "The phases".
28	
29	### A1. Before the tag
30	
31	- **[I] 21 of the 28 commits only put the tree on a current JDK and Scala toolchain** (build file, jars, generated sources, the fork-join pool): `8fe1daa8f`, `72716e6b0`, `c353a7676`, `22c059ef5` to `ac517a5ce`, `fdd4a57c2` to `439604f53`, `ef45a91ca` to `c4c90f936`, `561064bb1`, `760f7ea2a`. No Fortress-visible effect.
32	- The other 7 commits changed something a Fortress programmer or the suite sees. They are placed in their areas: `36d160799` (N8), `e700b442d` (X1), `4b1e500ca` and `e0f550094` (H1), `414b790e3`, `4672b71cd` and `9622f9db3` (SP9).
33	
34	### A2. The library's numbers
35	
36	- **N1 [V] The number types are siblings under `Number`, not a tower.**
37	  - The team left: `ZZ32` extends `ZZ64`, which extends `ZZ`; `NN32` extends `NN64`, which extends `ZZ`; `ZZ` reaches `AnyIntegral`, then `QQ`, then `RR64`; `RR32` extends `RR64`; `IntLiteral` extends `ZZ32` (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:335,370,406,434,461,495,533`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47,82,113`). The team's compiler prelude was already flat, each type excluding the others (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:102-443`).
38	  - Now: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` are siblings (`Number comprises { RR64, RR32, QQ, AnyIntegral }`, `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN64, NN32 }`), each with its own algebra; each wider type declares `coerce` from each narrower one. `RR64` converts from `ZZ32` and `RR32` only.
39	  - Commits: `d846e3644` (batch 6, rung F); `e455ccd98` for `RR32` (N11).
40	  - Decision: POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A)." and "Mixed widths convert by declared coercions (answer 8)."; FACTS, "The one library's number tower is flat"; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-6/RECORD.md`; PLAN, phase 2.
41	- **N2 [V] `SUM` and `PROD` are generic, and a sum's identity comes from the static argument.**
42	  - The team left: `opr SUM[\T extends Number\](g: Generator[\T\]): Number`, and the big operators `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN` over `Number` (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1820-1822,1842-1851`).
43	  - Now: one generic `SUM` and one `PROD` over the library's `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, the identity chosen by a `() -> T` witness `typecase`; the three `...N` operators are gone. A clause form whose element type nothing fixes writes its static argument: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] f(j)`. Two lines of the model program changed with it (`MicroGptFlat.fss:43` and `:28`, approved as diffs).
44	  - Commit: `d846e3644`.
45	  - Decision: POSITIONS, "`SUM` and `PROD` without the `Number` catch-all (answer 7)." and "The team demos that write no static argument for a generic reduction ..."; FACTS, "The one library's number tower is flat"; PLAN, phase 2.
46	- **N3 [V] `QQ` is exact.** The team left `QQ`'s `<` cross-multiplying its parts in whatever width they held, so fixed-width parts wrapped and `(widen(1) LSHIFT 62) < 1/4` was `true` (row 428). Now the parts are always `BigNum`. Commit `d846e3644`. Decision: row 428; FACTS, "The one library's number tower is flat".
47	- **N4 [V] Fixed-width arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk.**
48	  - The team left: the specification says overflow throws `IntegerOverflow` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:155,196`); the compiled natives did (`a874948ac:ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:64-80`); walk's natives wrapped (`.../interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:100-102`, `return x + y;`).
49	  - Now: walk's ten signed and eight unsigned natives raise the catchable `IntegerOverflow`; `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` too, and `CHOOSE` answers 0 for `k < 0` or `k > n`.
50	  - Commits: `917bb7b32` (batch 6b, rung O), `413f36ac0` (batch 6.5b, rung E, the powers).
51	  - Decision: POSITIONS, "Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under `walk`"; FACTS, "Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit, as the specification says"; `climb-batch-6b/RECORD.md`.
52	- **N5 [V] The specification's wrapping operators exist in the library.** The team's specification names `∔`, `∸` and `⨰` (wraparound `+`, `-` and `*`); no running library declared them (they were in a 2007 draft). Now `DOTPLUS`, `DOTMINUS` and `DOTTIMES` are declared on `Integral` and on the five integer types, bound to wrapping natives; the library bodies and six team tests that meant to wrap use them. Commit `ab914b6e0` (batch 5, rung D, landed as a follow-up). Decision: POSITIONS, "Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under `walk`" (the same entry); FACTS, "The specification's wrapping operators ∔, ∸ and ⨰ are declared in the interpreter's library, and the library bodies and team tests that meant to wrap use them".
53	- **N6 [V] Shifts, `GCD`, `LCM`, `narrow`.**
54	  - The team left, under walk: a negative shift count gave 0 or the sign, not a shift the other way (`a874948ac:ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:173-182`); `LCM` multiplied with a silent wrap (`.../Long.java:146-150`); `ZZ64.narrow` range-checked and refused a value outside `ZZ32` (`.../Long.java:237-240`).
55	  - Now, on both paths: `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` saturate at the width and shift the other way for a negative count; `shift` on `ZZ` is exact; `GCD` and `LCM` are nonnegative, with a catchable overflow; `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits; `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` no longer overflow. `ZZ32`'s shifts take a count of any integral type.
56	  - Commits: `d6faad28f` (walk) and `ce0c7f453` (compiled prelude), batch 3.5; `57600bc27`, batch 4, rung K; `413f36ac0`.
57	  - Decision: POSITIONS, "The integer principle.", "`LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` are bit operators; `shift` is exact on ℤ", "`GCD`/`LCM`", "`|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1`", "`narrow` out of range truncates"; FACTS, "The compiled path's integer rules" and "The interpreter's integer rules".
58	- **N7 [V] `round` sends an exact half to the even integer under walk** (`round(2.5)` is 2, `round(-3.5)` is -4). The team's walk used `Math.round`. Commit `9782955b1` (batch 3, rung R). Decision: POSITIONS, "`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer"; row 329.
59	- **N8 [V] The constant `e` is the double nearest `e`**, `2.718281828459045`, not `2.7182818284590455` (`a874948ac:Library/Constants.fss:16`). The old value was tuned to the 2012 JDK's `exp(1.0)`. Commit `36d160799` (before the tag). No decision of the curator; the commit message gives the reason.
60	- **N9 [V] A size beyond `NN32` (or `ZZ32` for an `int`) is refused on both paths, and walk reads a size exactly.** Commit `413f36ac0`. Decision: POSITIONS, "Sizes."; FACTS, "A size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` is refused on both paths, and walk reads a size exactly".
61	- **N10 [V] The numeral type `IntLiteral` is in the one library.** The team had `IntLiteral extends ZZ32` in the interpreter's library and a sibling `IntLiteral` in its prelude. Now the one library takes the prelude's: a sibling under `Number` that each integer type, `QQ` and `RR64` convert from, with each integer type's own comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`. Walk's numeral stays an `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by size until a later step. Commit `9d2e4c856` (batch 8, rung Q). Decision: POSITIONS, "The numeral switch, split by where the static types are."; FACTS, "The one library's numeral type is the compiler library's `IntLiteral` ...".
62	- **N11 [V] `RR32` is a sibling of `RR64`.** The team's `RR32` extended `RR64` and its natives took `RR64`; an `RR32` mixed with another number ended the run with an `InterpreterBug` (row 435). Now `RR64` converts from `RR32`. Commit `e455ccd98` (batch 6.5b, rung V). Decision: POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A)."; FACTS, "`RR32` is a sibling of `RR64` under `Number`, and `RR64` converts from it".
63	- **N12 [V] Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`.** Before, the inherited declaration's `self` was the generic trait, which converts into nothing: of 54 one-call programs, 16 stopped with "Ambiguous coercion" and 25 answered a `QQ`; now all answer at the promoted type. Commit `2770550c3` (batch N, rung M). Decision: POSITIONS, "Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`"; FACTS, "Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, so under `walk` the family answers at answer 8's type".
64	- **N13 [V] The comparisons, `Maybe` and `Condition` stop extending two instantiations of one trait.** `TotalComparison` extends `Comparison` alone (batch 7), then `StandardMinMax` beside it (batch 7b), so `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` over total comparisons answer again; `AnyMaybe` extends `AnyUniqueItem` alone; a second `ANDCOND` is renamed `andRelCond`, which makes a program's own `ANDCOND` of two relational predicates not relational under walk (row 458). Commits `952892a00` (batch 7, rung H), `070ef39e5` (batch 7b, rung L). Decision: POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A)." and "Appendix I's small items."; FACTS, "The compiled checker's exclusion rule is the designers' "multiple instantiation exclusion" ...".
65	- **N14 [V] `AnyIntegral` is closed.** The team left `trait AnyIntegral extends { QQ } end`. Now it comprises its five integer types (`comprises { ZZ }` at `02d09a39f`, the full list after the flattening). Commits `02d09a39f` (a probe worker, 09-19), `d846e3644`. Decision: POSITIONS, "`AnyIntegral`'s closure and how the checker reads `comprises`."
66	- **N15 [V] `StandardMinMax`'s `MIN` and `MAX` return one `T`.** The team declared them `(T,T)` (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:209-211`), a slip. Commit `de22fd928` (batch 7, rung B). Decision: row 421; `climb-batch-7/RECORD.md`.
67	
68	### A3. Ranges
69	
70	- **R1 [V] Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` alone.**
71	  - The team left: every range operator and trait was generic over any integer type, `opr #[\I extends AnyIntegral\](lo:I, ex:I): CompactFullRange[\I\]` and `trait ScalarRange[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2158-2185`, `Library/RangeInternals.fsi:44-480`).
72	  - Now: `RangeInternals` and the `#`, `:` and `::` operators declare no integer type parameter; every former `Integral` or `AnyIntegral` parameter is `ZZ32`. A numeral converts into it. A range over `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` or `ZZ` stops at its construction under walk; a wider counter widens a `ZZ32` index. The public range traits, `openRange` and the strided and sized operators on a `Range[\I\]` stay generic.
73	  - Commit: `3be1fecd7` (batch 7R, rung J). Specification side: SP5.
74	  - Decision: POSITIONS, "Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only"; FACTS, "The one library's scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` alone"; `climb-batch-7R/RECORD.md`.
75	- **R2 [I] The range bodies answer at the integer bounds without wrapping.** With N4, three bodies that answered right at the bounds only by wrapping (`MIN # 0`, `MAX # 1`, the power-of-two split) are reordered on the checked operators; the answers are the same. Commit `413f36ac0` (batch 6.5b, rung E). Decision: FACTS, "The one library's scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` alone" (rows 450 and 451).
76	- **R3 [V] Each range type declares the meet of its overload pairs.** `BoundedScalarRange`'s `CAP`, the two `CAP` of the left, right and full ranges of rank 2 and 3, `FullRange`'s abstract `IN`, `Just`'s `SQCAP` are declared on the meet; the full sequential ranges' `map` answers a new `SimpleMappedSeqIndexed`, whose rendering changes (row 603); 55 range slips are repaired to the types their bodies answer. Commit `631fb867e` (batch 9, rung R). Decision: FACTS, "The one library's range types provide a declaration on the meet for each of their Meet Rule pairs, and the range slips take the types their bodies answer".
77	- **R4 [V] `openRange` chooses among the three numbered ranges by a `typecase` on its witness**, where three helpers told apart only by arrow types stood (row 553). Commit `070ef39e5` (batch 7b, rung L). Decision: POSITIONS, "The static-parameter sentence goes (answer 9)."
78	
79	### A4. Arrays
80	
81	- **AR1 [V] `fill` takes a value, `tabulate` takes a function.**
82	  - The team left: both forms were named `fill`, `fill(f:I->E)` and `fill(v:E)`, declared in four array traits (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1294-1295,1313-1314,1333-1334,1365-1366`). For an element type of `Any` or a function type both apply and neither is more specific: the compiled checker refused the pair 302 times, and walk called a function meant as a value.

The team's library has `Monoid` only inside a comment (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2823`, between `(*************` and `*************)`) and in `Library/incomplete/`. The revival changed none of it. So pre-training remembers the specification correctly, and the quiz's own header says the source tree is the authority.
276	- **"`Any` does not include tuples" (guess; grade: wrong).** **Verdict: wrong for the team; the revival makes it matter.** Wrong for the team: the frozen text says `Any` comprises tuple types, arrow types, `()` and `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`). The revival changed the implicit bound of a type parameter to `Any` (point 5), which makes the fact matter.
277	- **"Overload-set validity is checked statically, per pair ... for any two overloads one of three must hold" (grade: outdated).** **Verdict: the team's Fortress, changed by the revival.** The team's Fortress: the three rules and the sentence that static parameters may not differ are the frozen specification's text (`overloading.tex:102-106`); walk checked at load (`OverloadedFunction.java:434-549`). The revival changed the model (point 2). Pre-training holds the team's.
278	- **"The interpreter ran tasks on a pool derived from `jsr166y`" (grade: outdated).** **Verdict: the team's Fortress, changed by the revival for a JDK reason.** Team: `a874948ac:ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/tasks/BaseTask.java:17` imports `jsr166y.RecursiveAction`. Revival: both pools extend `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool` (`2ed045233`, before the tag, a JDK change). Pre-training holds the team's.
279	- **"Some wrapping or modular types may have existed separately" (guess; grade: wrong).** **Verdict: wrong for both.** Wrong for both. The specification wraps by operators, `∔ ∸ ⨰` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:172-176` in the frozen text), not by types; the team's running library declared none of them (FACTS, "What relies on fixed-width wrapping under `walk`, and the wrapping operators no running library declares"); the revival declared them (N5). The audit is right.
280	- **"The interpreter implemented a subset of these [coercion] rules" (guess; grade: outdated).** **Verdict: wrong for the team (none, not a subset); the revival added it.** Wrong for the team, not merely outdated: walk implemented none. `a874948ac:.../interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:792` is a "TODO add checks for COERCE"; `grep -i coerc` over `interpreter/` finds two comments. The compiled checker had coercion (the `test-coercion` command, `CoercionOracle.scala`). The revival added walk's (W1). Pre-training is wrong about the team and right about the revival's direction.
281	- **"`CC` (complex) is in the spec, and the library implementation was partial" (grade: wrong).** **Verdict: half the team's specification; wrong for its library; the revival changed nothing.** Half right for the team. The specification names complex numbers (`types-vals-vars.tex:511-521`) and has a stub chapter (`basic-integers.tex:923`). No library had any (`git grep -w CC` over `Library/*.fsi` and the builtin api finds nothing). The revival changed nothing.
282	- **"An algebraic hierarchy `Associative[\T, ⊕\]`, `Monoid`, `Group`, `Ring`, `Field`, with laws in `property` declarations" (grade: wrong for the library).** **Verdict: the team's specification; wrong for its library; unchanged.** Same as the first claim: the specification's chapter, not the library. `property` runs on neither path, which is the team's (point 11).
283	- **"Run with something like `fortress run Foo.fss`" (grade: wrong).** **Verdict: the team's specification, not the team's tool; unchanged.** Describes the team's specification: `Specification-1.0-frozen/preliminaries/overview.tex:62,83` ("`fortress run HelloWorld.fss`", abbreviated `fortress`). Not the team's tool: its own usage text says `fortress [walk] ... somefile.fss` runs the interpreter and `fortress run somecomponent` runs a compiled component (`a874948ac:ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:149,195,198`), and `bin/fortress` sends `run` to `bin/run`, which starts `MainWrapper` on compiled classes. `bin/fortress` is unchanged by the revival. So pre-training holds the specification, and the specification disagrees with the tool, in the team's own tree.
284	- **"A large directory of `.fss` test programs with expected output was the regression suite" (grade: wrong).** **Verdict: partly the team's (compiled-path keys), wrong for the interpreter corpus.** Partly the team's. The team's interpreter corpus is 385 `.fss` programs with no expected-output file: a program passes if it throws nothing (`a874948ac:ProjectFortress/tests/`; the one oracle, `printing/test_oracle.txt`, is compared by `concurrentPrinting.sh`, which no build target runs). But the team's compiled-path tests are `.test` files that pin expected strings in their keys: 222 `compile_out_equals`, 27 `run_out_equals`, 16 `run_out_contains` in `compiler_tests/` (`git grep` at `a874948ac`). So "expected output" is right for the team's compiled-path tests, in their keys, and wrong for the interpreter corpus. The revival keeps the team's `.test` keys and asserts values inside its own tests (POSITIONS, "The suite's verdict is the check."). The audit's "wrong" is too strong.
285	- **Trap 5, "Overloading is dynamic multiple dispatch, statically checked" (grade: correct for the compiled path, outdated for walk).** **Verdict: both.** Walk checked at load in the team's tree (point 2). The revival widened the load check (W5, W6). Describes both.
286	
287	### B3. Rows the audit grades correct that hold only in part
288	
289	These are claims where the audit says "correct" and then notes a revival change. They answer the curator's question the other way round: pre-training is right about the team and the skill is right about the tree.
290	
291	- **"Fixed-width integer overflow throws an exception rather than wrapping."** Right for the specification and the team's compiled path; wrong for the team's walk (N4). The revival made walk agree.
292	- **"Ranges `a:b`, `a#n`, strided and open forms."** Right for the team, whose ranges were over any integer type; the revival's are over `ZZ32` (R1).
293	- **"`SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG op` reductions."** Right for the team; the revival's `SUM` is generic (N2).
294	- **"`ZZ32`, `ZZ64` fixed width; `NN32`, `NN64` naturals ..." and the missing row on how they relate.** The quiz does not say how they relate. A reader who assumes Haskell's classes or Java's widening, "narrower below wider", is describing the team's interpreter library exactly (point 6). The skill's "siblings, not a tower" is the team's compiler prelude and the revival's library.
295	- **"Static parameters `nat`, `int`, `bool`."** Specified by the team; implemented on the compiled path by the revival (C1, G5).
296	- **"Integer literals have type `IntLiteral`."** Right for the team's prelude and the checker; the one library's `IntLiteral` is the revival's (N10); walk's numerals are still `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum`.
297	
298	### B4. What follows
299	
300	- **Where pre-training is the team's Fortress and the skill is the revival's.** The nested number tower (walk's library); wrapping `+` under walk; no coercion in walk; ranges over any integer type; the static-parameter sentence in overloading; `jsr166y`; implicit bound `Object` in the specification text; the specification's algebra chapter and `fortress run`. Each is in B1 to B3 with its file and line.
301	- **Where the skill states a revival decision as the language.** Point 5 (the implicit bound `Any`, the unfixed parameter's bound), the reading of `comprises` in point 4, walk's load checks in point 2, overflow under walk and the flat interpreter library in point 6, and the one-thread suites in point 7. Each is true of the tree and of the standard as the revival revises it; none is true of the frozen specification.
302	- **What would settle the grade of two rows.** The quiz's claim on `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]` and `fortress run` are right about the specification and wrong about the tree. The audit grades them "wrong". If the standard is the revised specification (POSITIONS, "The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it."), those two are right; the audit's grade follows the tree.
303	- **Decision not taken: mark whose each point is.** The skill's eleven points do not say which are the team's and which the curator's. A reader of the skill cannot tell a rule of the language from a decision that can be revised. Alternatives: (a) leave as is; (b) add a clause to each point naming the decision (POSITIONS title) where it is the revival's, as B1 does. I did not edit the skill. The curator decides.
304

content.content: 211 27953 .claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md

1	# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress
2	
3	The team left three forms of Fortress, which disagree in places:
4	
5	- the specification;
6	- walk, with the interpreter's library;
7	- the compiled path, with the compiler's library.
8	
9	This part lists each change of the revival made for one of two reasons: two of the team's sources contradict each other, or a program failed. Its headings are the points of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", that the changes qualify.
10	
11	Each resolution is the rule of this tree. Follow it as you follow a decision of the curator, and question it only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Where it changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. `specification.md`, "Weighing the sources", describes the type group, whose later texts most resolutions follow.
12	
13	If a source of the team's, an old note or your training disagrees with this skill, find the point below. If it is there, follow the skill: it describes the tree. If it is not, do as `SKILL.md`, "When to explore", says.
14	
15	A note written before the revival, and your training, can be right about the team's walk and out of date here. Three examples: the number types form a tower, fixed-width arithmetic wraps, and walk converts no argument.
16	
17	## Dispatch is on every argument, at run time
18	
19	**Overloads that differ in static parameters**
20	
21	- Original: the Working Draft forbids two declarations of one name whose static parameters differ, beside the team's note "This restriction will be relaxed." Neither implementation enforced it, and the checker implements the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which allows them.
22	- Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the paper's model.
23	- Reason: the implementations and the library already allow such overloads. Enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
24	
25	**The return-type rule**
26	
27	- Original: the type group's 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one instance, so a pair that broke the rule compiled, and its run failed the JVM's verification.
28	- Resolution: the checker tests every instance.
29	- Reason: the paper's rule. Such a program now fails at compile time, not at run time.
30	
31	**Walk's choice between a generic and a plain declaration**
32	
33	- Original: the Working Draft chooses the most specific declaration by the declared parameter types. Walk chose by the order in which the declarations were written.
34	- Resolution: walk chooses by the declared types.
35	- Reason: the specification's rule. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
36	
37	**`fill` and `tabulate`**
38	
39	- Original: the interpreter's library declared two array methods named `fill`: one takes a value, one a function of the index. For an element type of `Any` or of a function type, both apply and neither is more specific. The checker refused the pair, and walk called a function meant as the value.
40	- Resolution: the function form is `tabulate` (`library.md`).
41	- Reason: a second name ends the ambiguity. Scala's `Array.fill` and `Array.tabulate` have the same two meanings.
42	
43	## Traits and objects, no classes
44	
45	**The exclusion rule**
46	
47	- Original: the type group's papers and the checker have the exclusion rule. The Working Draft does not state it, and some of its examples break it.
48	- Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed".
49	- Reason: without it, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`. The later Types chapter states the rule too.
50	
51	**What a `comprises` clause says**
52	
53	- Original: four passages of the Working Draft read the clause as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs that it allows. The type group's later Types chapter reads the clause as a statement about values.
54	- Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. A generic trait may extend the closed trait without being listed, if each type that extends it is below a listed type.
55	- Reason: read by values, the passages hold for those programs.
56	
57	**A trait's `override`, and object expressions, under walk**
58	
59	- Original: walk dropped an inherited declaration only where the object itself declared the `override`, so an object below a trait that overrides ran the overridden declaration. Its load check of the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Meet Rule") skipped object expressions: anonymous objects written inside an expression, such as `object extends { A, B } end`.
60	- Resolution: a trait's `override` declarations override for every type below it. Walk reads what each trait provides by the rule of "What a type provides", below, as its load check does. Walk lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function. It checks the lifted object as it checks an object. Walk checks a trait, object or lifted object with static parameters through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). It does not check a pair of declarations whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. Walk makes no stand-in, and so no Meet Rule check, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where it cannot make the type. The checker still accepts an object expression that breaks the rule (ledger row 570).
61	- Reason: the traits chapter (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Method Declarations"), and the Meet Rule, which names object expressions.
62	
63	**An abstract method without a body, and an `override` that overrides nothing, under walk**
64	
65	- Original: the traits chapter makes both static errors. An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only if the inherited declaration's parameter type is a strict subtype of the `override`'s, so an `override` at equal parameter types overrides nothing. Walk loaded both: a call of the abstract method stopped with an `InterpreterBug`, "has neither body nor def", and the `override` ran. The compiled checker refuses the first and accepts the second (ledger row 653).
66	- Resolution: walk refuses at load an object or object expression without static parameters that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body. In every trait, object and object expression, it refuses at load an `override` that overrides nothing, also one at the inherited declaration's own parameter types. It checks a trait, object or object expression with static parameters once, at its declaration, through the stand-in of "A trait's `override`, and object expressions, under walk". There it does not refuse an `override` of an inherited declaration whose parameter types differ from the `override`'s and mention a static parameter with bounds that walk does not read: an object expression's, which walk lifts without the `where` clauses around it, or one of a declaration that extends a type under a `where` clause (ledger row 693). An instance of a generic trait above a declared object is also checked at its static arguments, where equal parameter types count as overridden. So an `override` is not refused where those arguments make its parameter types equal to the inherited declaration's. A declaration with a body of the method's name, whose parameter types are the abstract declaration's or below them, counts as defining the abstract method (ledger row 666). This allowance departs from the chapter, which asks an object to define a body for the abstract method itself. A call outside the narrower types still stops walk with "has neither body nor def" (ledger rows 668 and 669). Walk makes no abstract-method check on a generic object (ledger row 665).
67	- Reason: the chapter's rules. Counting a body at narrower parameter types keeps the library loading: its `Pairs` component's `SingleRange` defines `RunRanges`'s abstract `BOXPLUS` only at the two types that `RunRanges`'s `comprises` clause lists. From their source, `QuickCheck`'s generators (ledger row 669) and `Random`'s `MersenneTwisterInit` (ledger row 668) need it too: each provides a body for an abstract method of a trait above it only at a narrower parameter type.
68	
69	**What a type provides**
70	
71	- Original: the traits chapter says that a type provides the method declarations it declares and inherits, and that it does not inherit one that its own `override` declaration overrides or whose parameter types its own declaration repeats. The compiled checker read every declaration of every supertype as provided, and refused the team's `ProjectFortress/tests/disp0.fss`, whose `override` widens a parameter.
72	- Resolution: both paths read what a type provides as the chapter says. The checker checks that the return type of an overriding declaration is a subtype of the return type of the declaration that it overrides.
73	- Reason: the specification's rule, which walk follows (above). The team's own test is valid by it.
74	
75	**A string's `left` and `right`**
76	
77	- Original: the interpreter's library declared `String`'s getters `left` and `right`, its first and last characters, as `Maybe[\Char\]`, but answered the character itself, so walk printed `a` for `"abc".left`. The specification is silent.
78	- Resolution: they answer `Just` of the character, and `Nothing` for the empty string, as `List`'s and the ranges' do.
79	- Reason: the declared type, which the checker enforced by refusing both bodies.
80	
81	## Static parameters
82	
83	**The bound of a type parameter that has none written**
84	
85	- Original: the Working Draft bounds it by `Object`. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, such as arrays indexed by pairs, and `Object` holds no tuple.
86	- Resolution: the bound is `Any`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path").
87	- Reason: the library works only with `Any`.
88	
89	**A type parameter that a call does not fix**
90	
91	- Original: the implementations gave it the empty type `Bottom`, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's verification. The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives such a parameter its bound.
92	- Resolution: it takes its bound on both paths. Under walk, one whose bound names itself stays open (the next entry). Walk still gives `Bottom` to these:
93	  - a big operator's static parameters with a plain bound (ledger row 424);
94	  - a parameter declared with two bounds, neither below the other (ledger row 591);
95	  - a parameter that an argument bounds only from above, whose bound names another static parameter (ledger row 612);
96	  - a parameter that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (ledger row 587).
97	- Reason: the paper is the type group's latest word on the rule.
98	
99	**A type parameter whose bound names itself, under walk**
100	
101	- Original: walk gave such a parameter the empty type `Bottom` where a call did not fix it, as `SUM`'s `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` in `SUM[i <- 1#100] i`. The reduction then refused its first element. The POPL 2019 paper's rule has no bound to give: such a bound is not a type until the parameter is known.
102	- Resolution: walk leaves the parameter open. Wherever walk checks a value against the open parameter, every value passes, so the reduction runs on the types of its elements. An empty reduction gives `ZZ32`'s identity, whatever the type of its elements (ledger row 645). A generic type that holds the open parameter admits no more than it admits at `Bottom`. So `Set`'s `BIG UNION` and `BIG INTERSECTION` still stop at their first element, which `Set[\OPEN\]` does not admit (ledger row 662). A printed type shows the open parameter as `OPEN`: `BoxU[\OPEN\]` for an object `BoxU[\T\]`. The checker still refuses the call (ledger row 425).
103	- Reason: walk has no static types, so it cannot take the element type from the static type of the reduced expression, as the specification's desugaring does (`Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex`). An open parameter refuses no element.
104	
105	**Sizes on the compiled path**
106	
107	- Original: the Working Draft has the size parameters `nat` and `int`. The checker crashed on sized declarations, and a sized program did not compile or load. The team's code generator had reserved a slot for a size's run-time descriptor.
108	- Resolution: the checker checks sizes, and the slot holds the size's descriptor (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time").
109	- Reason: it completes the team's design, which carries a size as it carries a type argument.
110	
111	**Arithmetic in a size**
112	
113	- Original: the Working Draft allows a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, and fixes its value once the static parameters are known, but does not say when two such sizes are the same. The checker refused any arithmetic in a size, and counted a static parameter as different from every numeral. The compiled path spelled the expression into the class's name.
114	- Resolution: two sizes are the same when they are written alike once each operation on numerals is computed: `2 3` is `6`, and, for static parameters `s0` and `s1`, `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter, or an expression with one in it, is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...`, for a static parameter `b0` and `NatReflect`'s object `N` (below), the arm `N[\0\]` is reachable. The checker checks a computed size against its parameter's kind, as it checks a numeral. It computes a power of 0, 1 or -1 at any exponent, and of another base up to the exponent 4096. It refuses a larger power as outside every kind. The compiled path computes a size when it names a class, so `Box[\2 + 1\]` and `Box[\3\]` are one class; the class loader does not check a size that it computes against its parameter's kind (ledger row 675). Walk computes a sum, a difference and a product, and stops on a power (ledger row 676).
115	- Reason: the library writes a product in the storage of its matrices, `mem: PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1)\]` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, and sums in result types. The team's questions and answers in the specification's appendix "Internal Document" (`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex`) refuse two overloads at `T[\n+1\]` and `T[\0\]`.
116	
117	**A size known only at run time**
118	
119	- Original: `NatReflect`'s `reflect` answers a `NatParam`, a trait that the object `N[\nat n\]` extends (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`). The team's clause of `NatParam`, `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]`, was a comment, and the api's comment says that a `NatParam` passed where `N[\n\]` is expected makes `n` a static parameter. The checker refused every such call in the library; walk ran them, binding the size at dispatch.
120	- Resolution: the clause is restored, and the specification allows a where-clause variable in a listed type. In the checker, a value of such a trait, passed where the listed type is expected, binds the call's `nat` parameter to the value's own size. That size is known to equal only itself: two values passed in one call have two sizes, and the size does not reach a type that names another size. Walk loads the clause and binds each size at dispatch, as before, so it runs such a call. The compiled run waits for the switch-over (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenRun.fss`).
121	- Reason: the team's comment, and the library's run-time factories, which pass `reflect`'s value to functions that take `N[\n\]`.
122	
123	**Comparing pairs and triples**
124	
125	- Original: the interpreter's library compared pairs and triples lexicographically with `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP` over element types with no bound, under the team's comment "Shouldn't these operators have to extend something? A,B,C?". Walk compared an element only when the elements before it were equal, so `((1,2),3) < ((1,3),0)` and `(1,()) < (2,())` were `true`. A pair whose first elements were unordered, such as a NaN against a float, stopped walk.
126	- Resolution: each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`, and walk refuses at the call a pair or triple with an element of another type, such as a pair or `()`, whatever the elements before it decide. Walk also refuses a pair whose elements at one position are numbers of two run-time types, such as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)`, which it answered `true`: it takes the element type at their join, which is no partial order (ledger row 511). A pair or triple whose deciding elements are unordered answers `false` to `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, and `Unordered` to `CMP`. `Reflect`'s `members` is a list in the order the type declares its members, not a set sorted by name: the set compared its triples, which the bound refuses.
127	- Reason: the checker refused the bodies of the ten operators, five on pairs and five on triples, at 17 sites. The team bounded the range points' comparisons `PCMP` and `SCMP` per element in 2008, and `false` is what `RR64`'s own comparisons answer for a NaN.
128	
129	## Numbers are siblings, not a tower
130	
131	**Tower or siblings**
132	
133	- Original: the interpreter's library nested the number types: `ZZ32` extended `ZZ64`, which extended `ZZ`. The compiler's library had them as siblings. The tower breaks the exclusion rule: `ZZ32` was an `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and, through `ZZ64`, an `Integral[\ZZ64\]`.
134	- Resolution: the library makes them siblings, as the compiler's library does.
135	- Reason: the exclusion rule stays (above), so the tower cannot.
136	
137	**Conversion under walk**
138	
139	- Original: the Working Draft converts a call's arguments by coercion when that makes the call apply, and the checker does so. Walk converted nothing: its dispatch code held the team's note "TODO add checks for COERCE".
140	- Resolution: walk converts by coercion at a call, a typed binding and an assignment. `interpreter.md` says how it chooses the coercion.
141	- Reason: the specification's rule, which the siblings need for every mix of widths.
142	
143	**Mixed number types in a generic call**
144	
145	- Original: neither implementation inferred a static argument through a conversion, and the Working Draft's chapter on inference is a heading and two notes. The tower needed no conversion there: a `ZZ32` was a `ZZ64`.
146	- Resolution: if the arguments of one type parameter mix number types, it takes the narrowest type into which all of them convert. For a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` that is `ZZ64`, and for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` too. Walk does not apply this rule to the elements of a tuple or varargs argument: it takes their join (ledger row 511). So it refuses `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` ("Comparing pairs and triples").
147	- Reason: among siblings, only a conversion joins two widths.
148	
149	**Overflow**
150	
151	- Original: the Working Draft and the compiled path raise `IntegerOverflow` when a fixed-width result does not fit. Walk wrapped the result.
152	- Resolution: walk raises `IntegerOverflow` too. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators (`library.md`).
153	- Reason: the specification and the compiled path already agreed.
154	
155	**Ranges**
156	
157	- Original: the interpreter's ranges took any integer type. The compiler's library had ranges over `ZZ32` only.
158	- Resolution: ranges are over `ZZ32` only (`library.md`).
159	- Reason: a range counts the indices of an array, and a JVM array index is a 32-bit `int`.
160	
161	**Bounded ranges of rank 2 and 3**
162	
163	- Original: the interpreter's library named a bounded range of rank 1, `BoundedScalarRange`, and none of rank 2 or 3, whose indices are pairs or triples of `ZZ32`. Its generic range traits, such as `RangeWithExtent[\I\]` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, compared indices of their type parameter, which declares no comparison. `|#(0,3)|` was 1, and walk stopped on `((0,0)#).every(-1,-1)`.
164	- Resolution: `BoundedRange2D` and `BoundedRange3D` name them. The range types over `ZZ32` of each rank, in `Library/RangeInternals.fsi`, declare the comparisons `CMP` and `FORWARD_CMP`, and the generic range traits declare them abstract. `#(0,n)` is empty, and a range made by a prefix `#` is declared a `RangeWithExtent`.
165	- Reason: the checker refused the ranges' declarations at 36 sites, and walk stopped or answered a wrong size. The library's range types of rank 1 gave the design.
166	
167	**Checking a range of rank 2 or 3 against bounds**
168	
169	- Original: the interpreter's library checked a range against an array's bounds (`narrowToRange`, through `checkSelection`) with its index type's `<` and `>`, which compare pairs and triples lexicographically. `((0,0):(9,9)).narrowToRange((2,-1):(5,5))` answered `(2,0):(5,5)` and raised no `IndexOutOfBounds`, so an array's range subscript of rank 2 or 3 with a corner outside the bounds on an axis after the first was cut to the bounds, and a subarray read past them.
170	- Resolution: the check compares corner by corner, by the ranges' own point order `PCMP`, under which one point is below another only if it is below or equal on every axis. The call above raises `IndexOutOfBounds`, as do such subscripts and subarrays. The check is one function for each rank, `checkSelection`, `checkSelection2D` and `checkSelection3D` in `Library/RangeInternals.fss`, and `narrowToRange`'s bodies are declared at the range types over `ZZ32` of each rank.
171	- Reason: the lexicographic order serves sorting, and a corner outside the bounds on any axis is outside them.
172	
173	**The trivial open range `(:)`**
174	
175	- Original: `(:)` is a range over `Any`. The interpreter's library gave its `truncL`, `truncR`, `every`, `imposeStride` and `atMost` bodies that answer ranges over `ZZ32`: `(:).truncL(3)` was `3#`.
176	- Resolution: the five throw `FailCalled`, through the library's `fail`, with a message that names `(:)`, and so do `(:):s` and `(:)#n`, which call two of them. `(:)` as a whole subscript, `a[:]`, is unchanged.
177	- Reason: each of the five declared types is a range over `Any`. Generics are invariant, so the old bodies' ranges over `ZZ32` broke those types, and the checker refused them.
178	
179	**`SUM` and `PROD`**
180	
181	- Original: `SUM` and `PROD` reduced over `Number`, under the team's comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically". Every sum had the type `Number`, and an empty sum of `RR64` values was the integer 0.
182	- Resolution: each is one generic declaration over the element type's own algebra, which gives its zero or one at that type (`library.md`).
183	- Reason: `Number`'s operators for any number went with the tower, so each reduction uses the element type's own operator.
184	
185	**Rounding a rational at an infinity or 0/0**
186	
187	- Original: the Working Draft (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers") gives `QQ`'s `floor`, `ceiling`, `round` and `truncate` the result type ℤ, and a later paragraph of that section says they return the argument at +∞, −∞ and 0/0, a rational. The interpreter's library returned the argument, and its `round` stopped walk there.
188	- Resolution: these methods and the brackets ⌊ ⌋ and ⌈ ⌉ throw `DivisionByZero` at those three values.
189	- Reason: the declared result type is ℤ, and a division by zero whose result is an integer throws `DivisionByZero` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators").
190	
191	## Loops and reductions are library code
192	
193	**The lifted type of a reduction without an identity**
194	
195	- Original: the interpreter's library lifted the reductions without an identity, such as `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG //`, to the type `AnyMaybe`, which takes no type argument. Such a reduction wraps each element in a `Just` with its `lift`, joins two wrapped elements by its `simpleJoin` of their contents, and answers `Nothing` for no element. Their `simpleJoin` took and answered `Any`, and their `lift` took `Any`, while `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` declared `lift(r:R)`. The team's tests declared their own such reductions with `simpleJoin` at `Any`, and passed `AnyMaybe` to `generate` as its static argument.
196	- Resolution: `AssociativeReduction[\R\]` lifts to `Maybe[\R\]`. Its `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`, and every `lift` takes `R`. A reduction that extends it declares `simpleJoin` at its element type. Under walk, one declared at `Any` or with untyped parameters leaves the abstract `simpleJoin` without a body: walk refuses such a reduction at load, and one with static parameters stops at its first join. A static argument that names the lifted type is `Maybe[\R\]`, as in `h.generate[\Maybe[\(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\](TestReduction, sing)` in `ProjectFortress/tests/HeapTest.fss`.
197	- Reason: the checker refused the library's declarations at `Any` in 13 places, and `join`'s `if av <- a` cannot bind from `AnyMaybe`, which is not a `Condition`, a generator of zero or one element. `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Set`'s `Intersection` already wrote these types. The declarations at `Any` had kept some of walk's reductions running while walk gave `Bottom` to a type parameter that a call did not fix. Walk now leaves such a parameter open only if its bound names itself. With a plain bound, it still gives `Bottom`, so `BIG SQCAP`, `BIG SQCUP` and `List`'s `BIG CONCAT` without static arguments stop at their first element (ledger row 424).
198	
199	**A generator's size, the relational predicate and the default index-value pairs**
200	
201	- Original: the interpreter's library declared no size on `Generator`, though three of the library's bodies read the size of a `Generator`. The relational predicate, the condition that `relationalPredicate(r)` makes (`RelationalPredicateCondition`'s `cond` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`), asks whether `r` holds between each two consecutive elements of its target, a `Generator`; it read a size and indices from 0 off the target. Under walk, `|g|` of a filter, a nest or a mapped filter stopped, and so did the relational predicate on a filter; on an array whose indices start above 0 it read outside the bounds. `Indexed`'s default `indexValuePairs` answered a mapped generator, printed `mapped(...)`, where an `Indexed` is declared. The checker refused these at nine sites.
202	- Resolution: `Generator` has `opr |self|`, a default that counts the elements by running the generator, as `opr IN` searches them. A type with its own size keeps it. The relational predicate is one reduction in the generator's natural order, as the relational reduction of `Generator2` (`efficientImplRelationalDistributiveImpl` in `Library/Generator2.fss`) is. The default pairs are an object over the indexed value, `SimpleIndexValuePairs`, which prints as its elements and is indexed as the value is; a slice of it keeps each pair's index. So two answers change under walk: the relational predicate on a reversed indexed value follows its natural order, and the default pairs of a value indexed from 5 are indexed from 5, not from 0.
203	- Reason: the checker's refusals. A default keeps "only needs to define the generate method" true (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`). Counting consumes a consumable generator and never ends on an endless one, as every other derived default of `Generator` does.
204	
205	## Specified, but not built
206	
207	**A parameter whose type is left out**
208	
209	- Original: the components chapter (`Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex`) says that type inference finds every type that a component leaves out. The compiled checker refused a top-level function's or a method's parameter written without a type, and crashed on a local function's. Walk runs such declarations, except a method that implements an abstract declaration, which stops at its first call (ledger row 405).
210	- Resolution: the compiled path refuses every such parameter of a top-level function, a method or a local function, with "Missing parameter type for" and the parameter's name. A `\revision` box in that file and Appendix I say so.
211	- Reason: no text describes that inference. A crash of the checker is no answer, and the refusal already stood at top level.

3	# The three specification artefacts: what each one is, and how they relate
4	
5	## Summary
6	
7	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` is the real 1.0 release artefact: added
8	  2008-03-31 by the team (`403afbe0b`). The LaTeX **sources** sitting next to it in
9	  `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are not 1.0 text — they are a January 2012 clone of the
10	  then-current working draft, made by Guy Steele, and they are still today the working
11	  draft in 202 of 208 tracked files.
12	- `Specification/` is that same working draft, carried forward. The team's last edit to
13	  its text is 2010-12-09. Nobody touched it again until the revival built and committed
14	  a rendered PDF from it in 2026, under the label "July 19, 2012" — a date the revival
15	  chose, not the team, and not the date of any edit.
16	- `Documentation/Specification/` is a separate, later, unfinished restart: begun
17	  2012-02-20 by Victor Luchangco, restructured and substantially written by Steele and
18	  Luchangco through May 2012, abandoned on 2012-05-31 with a 65-page draft PDF and most
19	  chapters still empty skeletons. Two of its finished chapters (Types, and part of
20	  Lexical Structure) are, by date, newer team prose than anything in `Specification/`.
21	
22	## 1. `fortress.1.0.pdf`: origin
23	
24	`fortress.1.0.pdf` entered the tree on 2008-03-31, added whole (22,280 lines of binary
25	diff) by Sukyoung Ryu at `Specification/fortress.1.0.pdf`, commit message "Added the
26	Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0." (`403afbe0b`). This is the team's own
27	2008 release artefact — the 1.0 spec that shipped with the matching interpreter release
28	(root `README.md:88`, "The 1.0 specification, with a matching interpreter release,
29	followed in March 2008") — not something the revival produced or found elsewhere. It is
30	262 pages (`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md:102`).
31	
32	It lived at `Specification/fortress.1.0.pdf` for almost four years. When Steele cloned
33	the whole `Specification/` directory into `Specification-1.0-frozen/` on 2012-01-04
34	(`c02fa44d0`), the clone copied this file along with everything else, so a second,
35	byte-identical copy came to exist at `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`. Both
36	copies sat in the tree, unedited, until the revival's `414b790e3` (2026-08-21) removed
37	the one at `Specification/fortress.1.0.pdf` as a duplicate — replacing it with the
38	revival's own freshly built `Specification/fortress.pdf` — and kept the one at
39	`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, which is the file the tree has today
40	(confirmed: `find . -iname fortress.1.0.pdf` returns exactly one hit, and
41	`git show --stat 414b790e3` shows `Specification/fortress.1.0.pdf | 22280 -----------`
42	removed in that commit).
43	
44	So: yes, it is the 2008 release artefact; the team committed it in 2008; the revival's
45	only act on it was to delete the second, redundant copy in 2026 — it did not touch the
46	surviving one.
47	
48	## 2. Why Steele froze the draft in January 2012
49	
50	`c02fa44d0` ("Cloned Specification directory into Specification-1.0-frozen", Guy Steele,
51	2012-01-04) sits inside a week of intense work by David Chase and Jean-Baptiste Tristan
52	on operator static parameters and RTTI (`b24a48a3c`, `4305f45d9`, `5d1c1b5ce`,
53	`30b00ab60`, all 2012-01-04 to 01-13) — none of it touching the specification. Nothing in
54	the surrounding commit messages states a reason for the clone.
55	
56	What the record does show is what happened *after*: the team never again edited
57	`Specification/`'s text (confirmed by the date-order tree walk below); instead, five and
58	a half weeks later, Victor Luchangco started a **different, new** directory,
59	`Documentation/Specification/` (`166841592`, 2012-02-20), and by May 2012 Steele had
60	joined him in restructuring and writing it (§3). Read against that sequence, the January
61	clone reads as Steele setting the existing draft aside — freezing it as a fixed
62	reference point — just before the team began rethinking the specification from scratch
63	rather than continuing to edit the old one. This is a reading of the sequence, not a
64	stated reason; no design note, README, or mailing-list text in the tree says so in words.
65	(`explorations/reviews/spec-change-form.md:237-239` reaches the same reading
66	independently: "Before a large revision (2012). Steele copied the whole directory ... and,
67	four months later, began a new document instead of editing the old one.")
68	
69	The name "1.0-frozen" is misleading taken literally. `git diff --quiet
70	2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds (verified directly)
71	— the clone is byte-for-byte the working draft as it stood on 2011-02-02, not the 1.0
72	text. Today the two source trees still differ in only 5 of 208 tracked files: the
73	revival's restyling of `fortress/fortress.tex` and its three `fortress/*.pl` table
74	generators (`4672b71cd`), and one historical stray `\tracingcommands=1\tracingmacros=1`
75	line at `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:17` that is absent from the frozen copy
76	(`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:109-111,117`). The only
77	genuinely-1.0 content near it is the PDF beside it (§1).

79	## 3. `Documentation/Specification/`
80	
81	**Started.** Victor Luchangco, 2012-02-20, `166841592`, "Added directory structure and
82	skeleton files for new spec (under new Documentation directory)" — twelve files, 948
83	lines, under a brand-new top-level path with its own `Root`, `Support`, `Prose`, `Code`,
84	`Data` layout (`Documentation/Specification/README.txt:12-19` names this structure).
85	Victor Luchangco added more skeleton on 2012-03-30 (`efa42d03a`, "mostly empty (except
86	for copyright info) .tex files"). Guy Steele restructured it again on 2012-05-07
87	(`37d7e5619`, "New directory structure for Documentation/Specificaation") and switched
88	its prose format from `.tex` to a `.tick` source format (fortick-processed, like the

102	- 2012-03-13 to 03-24: Tristan King builds the BNF-grammar tooling for the appendix

122	No commit after 2012-05-31 makes a real change to the directory; every later hit in a

126	**What it covers, and how far.** Its `Prose/` tree is 6.2K lines total, but most of that

138	**Was it meant to replace `Specification/`?** No explicit statement of intent survives in

228	## 6. The consequence: which artefact is the team's latest statement, topic by topic
229	
230	The project's goal names `Specification/` — "the July 2012 draft" — as the standard to
231	finish the language against. On the great majority of the language, this is simply
232	correct: `Specification/` is not only the largest and most complete of the three (596–599
233	pages against 262 for the 1.0 PDF and 65 for `Documentation/Specification/`'s last
234	build), it is also, on every topic `Documentation/Specification/` never got past a
235	12-to-30-line skeleton for, the team's only and therefore latest statement. That covers
236	static parameters (`trait-parameters.tex` — the exact chapter behind the multiple-
237	instantiation-exclusion question that prompted the batch-4 specification rung has **no**
238	corresponding file at all in `Documentation/Specification/Prose/`, skeleton or
239	otherwise), traits and objects beyond a stub, exceptions, components and APIs, the memory
240	model, parallelism, dimensions and units, and the entire numeric-tower library part.
241	
242	On two topics, though, `Documentation/Specification/` genuinely holds later team prose
243	(§3): **Types**, where `types.tick` (Victor Luchangco, 2012-05-31) is a complete,
244	from-scratch rewrite dated a year and a half after `Specification/`'s last edit to the
245	matching chapter; and, more partially, **Lexical Structure**, where a newer but
246	admittedly incomplete chapter exists alongside the older, fuller one. On these two
247	topics, if "the team's latest statement of the language" is read literally, it is the
248	unfinished `Documentation/Specification/` text, not `Specification/` — though that text
249	was never finished, never checked against the rest of the language definition, and never
250	adopted as the specification of record before the project ended. This is offered as
251	evidence bearing on Pavol's decision of what to cite where; it does not by itself say
252	which text should govern.

15.6      Overloading Rules for Functional Declarations

This section provides rules for valid functional overloading. If a pair of overloaded declarations satisfies any one
of the following three rules, it is considered a valid overloading. The overloading rules given in this section are

                                                           96
 disjoint; at most one rule applies to each pair of overloaded declarations. It is possible for new rules to be added which
allow additional overloadings. Valid overloadings for declarations that contain varargs parameters are determined by
analyzing the expansion of these declarations as described in Section 15.4. Therefore, varargs parameters are ignored
in the remainder of this section.


15.6.1    Type Relationships with Static Parameters

Before describing the overloading rules, we extend two type relations to take static parameters into account. For type
parameters, we use their bounds as their supertypes. As with the rest of this chapter, the type relations described in
this section may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented.

We say that type T is a subtype of U if any of the following holds:

   • neither type includes static parameters and T is a subtype of U (as described in Section 6.2),

   • U does not include any static parameters and any supertype of T that does not include a static parameter is a
     subtype of U (as described in Section 6.2).

We say that two types exclude each other if any of the following holds:

   • neither type can be extended,

   • one cannot be extended, and the other is not its supertype, or

   • their supertypes exclude each other.


15.6.2    Subtype Rule

If the parameter type of one declaration is a subtype of the parameter type of another (and they are not the same) then
there is no ambiguity between these two declarations: for every call to which both are applicable, the first is more
specific. This is the basis of the Subtype Rule.

The Subtype Rule also requires a relationship between the return types of the two declarations. Without such a
requirement, a program may violate type safety.

content.content:
- **Kotlin** forbids it ("inconsistent values" for a supertype's type parameter). Its numbers are flat, each `Comparable<Self>`, and widening is explicit (`toLong()`).
- **Swift** allows one conformance per protocol. Protocols carry `Self` and associated types, not type arguments, so two instantiations cannot even be written. `Int32` and `Int64` are separate structs under `BinaryInteger`, which is the self type used as a bound (Naden `:618-624`).
- **Rust** allows `impl From<u8> for u64` beside `impl From<u16> for u64`. Coherence allows at most one impl per trait and argument list, and the impl is chosen at compile time, so nothing picks an instantiation at run time. Its numbers are flat, with explicit `From`/`as`.
- **Haskell** allows one instance per type for a one-parameter class, and many for multi-parameter classes (an extension). Instances are resolved statically. Its numbers are flat instances of `Num`, with explicit `fromIntegral`.
- **C#** (not asked for; its generics are reified like Fortress's) allows `IEquatable<A>` and `IEquatable<B>` on one class. Overloads are resolved statically, and generic math uses `INumber<TSelf> where TSelf : INumber<TSelf>` on a flat tower with implicit widening.
- What this means for the tower: no peer combines nested numeric subtyping with self-typed traits; every one has a flat tower plus conversions. The peers that allow multiple instantiation choose the instantiation statically, which is the specification's call-site model. Naden's hole appears only with dispatch at run time over reified generics, which is Fortress's combination.

(** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.
    Define opr TIMES; juxtaposition is defined in terms of TIMES. **)
trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    abstract getter one(): T
    abstract opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T
    (** Exponentiation need only deal with natural exponents. **)
    opr ^(self, other:ZZ64): T
end

trait Number
        extends { StandardPartialOrder[\Number\], StandardMinMax[\Number\],
                  AdditiveGroup[\Number\], MultiplicativeRing[\Number\] }
        comprises { RR64 }
    opr =(self, b:Number):Boolean
    opr =/=(self, b:Number):Boolean
    opr <(self, b:Number):Boolean
    opr <=(self, b:Number):Boolean

- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 by Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
- **The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A).** "Agreed. Route A it is." The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule; the library's numeric tower is flattened as Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010: the fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` siblings under `Number`, each carrying its own algebra, `Number` without its catch-all operators, a `coerce` on each wider type converting from the narrower; the interpreter converts by coercion at dispatch; the specification is revised with a decision record that preserves the original text, the reasoning and route C. ℤ sits inside ℚ by coercion. Built. Reversal to route C costs what FACTS's route C entry lists. His readings while the fork was open stand: the patents' forest rule against the flattened prelude was "the team's last record on how to do the 'Fortress' way", the route culminating in the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule and specialisation by a run-time return-type check; and "without specialized code there will be no change at performance. But how a specialization is chosen 'ist mir egal', as long as it runs fast."
- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. The unrevised copy is called "the Working Draft of February 2011", in the team's own form, each citation giving the path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; Appendix I says once that the directory's name is misleading, since only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Appendix I's introduction says that the entries follow the revival's decisions, route A the first of them, each naming its own.
- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and 
- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.

content.content:
\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
\seclabel{revival-changes}
\sloppy

This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
open disagreement.
Each changed passage carries a box headed
``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.

Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
would require.
The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
there.
The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
Fortress~1.0 release.
The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
new one, is in the revival's decision records,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
and, for the number chapters,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
in the same repository.

Each change below follows a decision of the revival.
The first of those decisions, taken on
24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}, is that the compiled type checker keeps
the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
stated, and that the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
satisfy it.
An entry whose change does not follow from route~A says so, and names the
decision it follows or gives its reason.
The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
\secref{revival-routec}.

\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
\seclabel{revival-routec}

The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
instantiations when they form a chain.
The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
type checker and code generator.
Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
types.
Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
no chain contains.
Under route~C the numeric chapters could have kept the nesting of their
widths, and their original text, quoted in \secref{revival-numbers} and the
entries after it and kept in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's
for that nesting; route~C rescues neither the refined number types nor
\TYP{RationalQuantity} (\secref{revival-numbers}).
The record of the experiment is
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
revival's repository.
\fussy
